scenes.visual_description: On a dark canvas, the prediction question asks: 2 times faster FFT; how much faster overall? A second line invites a prediction before following the time. No numerical answer is shown yet.

A horizontal bar labelled BEFORE represents 100 milliseconds. Its first fifth is teal, labelled Fourier computation, 20 milliseconds; the remaining four fifths are amber, labelled other work, 80 milliseconds. Text states sequential work, same accuracy and no added overhead. These are assumptions of the synthetic model, not measured guarantees.

The original 100-millisecond bar stays above a second bar drawn on the same time scale. From 18 to 21 seconds only the second bar's teal Fourier segment shrinks from 20 to 10 milliseconds; the amber 80-millisecond segment keeps its length. During movement an arrow points toward 90 milliseconds: it labels the endpoint, not an instantaneous measured total. From 21 seconds the second bar is settled at 90 milliseconds. The captions state the resulting 10-millisecond saving.

The large equation reads: 100 divided by 90 is approximately 1.11 times. Below it, S = 1 / [(1 - f) + f/s]. In words, overall speedup equals one divided by the sum of the unchanged time fraction and the improved time fraction divided by its component speedup. Here f = 0.20 of baseline time and s = 2 for the Fourier component. The approximation sign matters: 100/90 is not exactly 1.11.

From 40 to 43 seconds the remaining teal segment shrinks toward zero. An arrow points toward the 80-millisecond endpoint, while the amber other-work segment remains unchanged. After 43 seconds the settled bar contains only that 80 milliseconds. The dark remainder is only the comparison bar's background; it does not add to the new duration. At 44.5 seconds the equation appears: 100 divided by 80 equals 1.25 times maximum. This ceiling belongs only to the stated model.

Four category titles remain visible in a horizontal strip. Every three seconds, a teal outline and a larger explanation panel move the focus to the next category, in the order below. The titles and words, not color alone, distinguish the questions.

A numbered checklist shows: accuracy and numerical error; data movement and alignment; worst-case deadlines and validation. An amber warning reads: Synthetic arithmetic. Not operational evidence. The footer continues to identify a synthetic example with no grid telemetry.

The source-only card says Measure the whole job and Synthetic - not a benchmark. Its concept path connects Fourier methods to component costs to end-to-end latency; these arrows locate the lesson, not an equivalence or readiness proof. A panel offers a public Python / Marimo notebook and explicitly labels it Source code only - not a live interactive app. Another line states Faster computation is not equal to validated grid readiness. Credits identify the model as synthetic and the accuracy context as the FFTW authors. The two final captions below point to source code and deny any live-lesson or real-grid benchmark claim.
